Masters|Masters]] (1901) * ''Gloriosa rothschildiana'' O'Brien (1903) * ''Gloriosa verschuurii'' Hoog (1950) * ''Gloriosa rockefelleriana'' Stehlé & Stehlé (1965) }} }} '''''Gloriosa superba'''''{{efn|name=Names|Also known as christmas flower, climbing lily, creeping lily, flame lily,{{GRIN |access-date=1 August 2026}} glory lily,{{cite web |last=Scheper |first=Jack |url=http://www.floridata.com/ref/g/glor_rot.cfm |title=''Gloriosa superba'' |work=Floridata |access-date=1 June 2026 }} and tiger claw.{{cite web |url=http://www.hear.org/pier/commonnames/details/gloriosa_superba.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230529180315/http://www.hear.org/pier/commonnames/details/gloriosa_superba.htm |archive-date=29 May 2023 |title=Common names, ''Gloriosa superba'' |publisher=[[Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]] |access-date=1 June 2026 }}}} is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Colchicaceae]]. It is native to and common across most of Africa except [[North Africa]], [[South Asia]], [[Southeast Asia]], and south-central China. It has been introduced to parts of Americas, Australia, and the [[Pacific Islands]]. The plant produces several solitary bright red and yellow coloured flowers on long stalks. Though most parts of the plant are highly [[poisonous]], it is used extensively in [[traditional medicine]]. ==Description== ''Gloriosa superba'' is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] that grows from a fleshy, horizontal, and white [[rhizome]].{{cite web |url=http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Gloriosa-superba.htm |title=''Gloriosa superba''. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606221835/http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Gloriosa-superba.htm |archive-date=6 June 2013 |publisher=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families, [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |year=2011 }}{{cite web |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/cropfactsheets/gloriosa.html |title=''Gloriosa superba'' |publisher=New Crop Resource Online Program, Center for New Crops & Plant Products, [[Purdue University]] |year=2002 }} It has a thin [[stem (botany)|stem]] measuring up to {{cvt|3 to 4|m}} in length in [[vine|climbing]] plants, while being shorter in erect plants. Unlike other plants from the [[lily]] family, the plant produces green colored leaf-tip [[tendril]]s which are {{cvt|2 to 3 |in}} long, which is used for holding on to surfaces. The leaves are either [[Phyllotaxis|arranged]] alternately or oppositely.{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200027670 |title=''Gloriosa superba'' |publisher=Flora of China |access-date=1 June 2026 }} The leaves are lance-shaped or elongated oval shaped with coiled lip tips with tendrils. The leaves are attached to the stem by a short [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]. The leaves are {{cvt|10.2 to 12.7|cm}} long, and {{cvt|1.3 to 2.5|cm}} wide, with smooth margins, and has several prominent veins running along the surface. The plant produces large solitary flowers measuring {{cvt|7.6 to 12|cm}} in length and {{cvt|4.5 to 7|cm}} in diameter. Each flower may weigh over {{cvt|2.5|g|oz|2}}.{{cite journal |url=http://epubs.icar.org.in/ejournal/index.php/JMAP/article/view/22885/pdf |title=Reproductive biology of ''Gloriosa superba'' |journal=Journal of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=5–11 |first1=A. |last1=Selvarasu |first2=R. |last2=Kandhasamy |year=2012 }} They are borne on slender and long [[pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s measuring up to {{cvt|20|cm}} in length. The flowers are [[actinomorphic]] and [[Monoicy|bisexual]]. The [[perianth]] consists of six {{cvt|5 to 8.3|cm}} long [[tepal]]s, which are elongated and [[spathulate|spoon shaped]] with wavy margins. The tepals are largely free and attached only at the base. When the small, green colored [[buds]] blossom, the tepals elongate and bend backwards while changing color. A mature flower shows a brilliant yellow to red colorization. Other variations with off white, yellow, orange, maroon, and purple-brown flowers have been reported. Each flower contains six prominent [[stamen]]s slanting outwards towards the tepals. The stamen consists of a {{cvt|1|cm}} long anther borne on the tip of a {{cvt|3 to 4|cm}} long filament, and the [[pollen]]s are released from vertical slits on the [[extrorse|exterior]] of the anther. The [[gynoecium]] consists of three carpels attached along the inner edge of the flower to form the pistil which holds a [[hypogynous|superior]] [[ovary]] on the top. Each pistil consists of a {{cvt|2.5 to 3.5|cm}} long style and {{cvt|6 to 7|mm}} long stigma. The fruit is a fleshy capsule up to {{cvt|6|cm}} long consisting of several red seeds. ==Distribution and ecology== [[File:Gloriosa superba distribution.png|thumb|Natural distribution (green)
Area of introduction (pale blue)]] The plant is native to Africa, tropical regions of [[South Asia]] and [[Southeast Asia]], and south-central China. In Africa, except [[North Africa]], it is found in most of the mainland, from Senegal in the east to Ethiopia in the west, and all the way down to South Africa.{{cite web |url=http://www.prota4u.org/downloads/Gloriosa+superba/Gloriosa+superba.pdf |title=''Gloriosa superba'' L. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714194421/http://www.prota4u.org/downloads/Gloriosa+superba/Gloriosa+superba.pdf |archive-date=14 July 2014 |publisher=Protabase Record Display, [[Plant Resources of Tropical Africa]] |first1=E. |last1=Dounias }} It has been [[introduced species|introduced]] to [[Alabama]] and [[Hawaii]] in the United States, parts of the [[Caribbean]], [[Suriname]] in South America, the Australian territories of [[New South Wales]], [[Queensland]], and [[Northern Territory]], and various [[Pacific Islands]]. Though it is distributed widely across South Asia and Africa, the species has been rarer in [[Southern Africa]], Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and certain territories of India. The decline is attributed to the harvesting of wild plants for its parts for usage in [[traditional medicine]]. On the other hand, outside its native range, it has been classified as an [[invasive species]] in Australia and the Pacific Islands such as [[Cook Islands]], [[French Polynesia]], [[Kiribati]], and Singapore.{{cite web |url=http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=V28 |title=''Gloriosa superba'' |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120205204036/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl |archive-date=5 February 2012 |publisher=Weeds Australia, National Weeds Strategy |first1=J. R. |last1=Thorp |first2=M. |last2=Wilson |year=1998 }} The plant is found across a variety of habitats including dense [[tropical forest]]s, [[savannah]], [[grassland]]s, [[dune]]s, edges of agricultural fields, barren lands, and on roadsides. It is generally found in the wild at altitudes ranging from {{cvt|900 to 1300|m}}, though it has been found at altitudes up to {{cvt|2500|m}}. In natural habitats, the plant is likely [[pollination|pollinated]] by [[butterfly|butterflies]] and [[sunbird]]s. ==Cultivation== {{Multiple image | align = right | total_width = 300 | image1 = Gloriosa superba 1DS-II 3-3511.jpg | image2 = Seed pod of Gloriosa superba (14872918441).jpg | footer = Fruit (left) and seeds in a dry pod | }} The plant is widely cultivated in South Asia, and in parts of Southeast Asia and Africa. The domestic [[cultivar]]s may vary in characteristics from the wild plants. There are dwarf varieties and plants producing flowers with broader and smoother tepals. Several color variations are cultivated including plants producing all white, orange, plum, or yellow flowers. The plant can be [[plant propagation|propagated]] by seed or [[vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] by dividing the rhizome. The sprouting of the seeds can take anywhere between a few weeks to three months. The seeds can sprout even after remaining dormant for up to nine months. The [[tuber]]s are divided every two years, and two-thirds of the tubers generally sprout within a month. However, an existing tuber can be used to propagate a maximum of two plants in a year. As plants grown from seeds can take long to germinate, and three years to mature, various methodologies, such as soaking the seeds in water, maintaining a warm and stable temperature while germinating, augmenting with chemicals such as [[hypochlorite]], and addition of growth hormones such as [[auxins]], are used to speed up the germination and growth of the plant. The plant grows well on moist and well drained soils with good sun light. Mature plants flower for about seven weeks during the rainy season, and the flower buds take about two weeks to bloom. The plant dies after a flowering season, and new shoots arise from the tuber again. Problems during cultivation include inadequate pollination, fungal diseases such as [[Cochliobolus lunatus|leaf blight]] and [[sclerotium|tuber rot]], crop pests such as the [[moth]]s ''Polytela gloriosa'' and ''[[Chrysodeixis chalcites]]'', [[louse|lice]], and [[thrips]]. A 2012 study reported that ''in vitro'' experiments with [[plant tissue culture]] increased the yield in few of the trials.{{cite journal |last1=Yadav |first1=Kuldeep |last2=Aggarwal |first2=Ashok |last3=Singh |first3=Narender |title=Actions for ''ex situ'' conservation of ''Gloriosa superba'' L. – an endangered ornamental cum medicinal plant |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12892-012-0045-7 |journal=Journal of Crop Science and Biotechnology |date=2012 |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=297–303 |doi=10.1007/s12892-012-0045-7}} The fruits are hand-picked and the tubers are dug out during harvest. The fruits are dried and split, and the seeds are removed and dried further. The seeds and rhizomes are sold as whole or in powdered or oil forms. ==Chemical composition and toxicity== [[File:Gloriosa superba 1.jpg|thumb|Most parts of the plant, including the flowers, are poisonous to humans]] The plant contains high levels of [[colchicine]], an [[alkaloid]], derived from the [[amino acids]] [[phenylalanine]] and [[tyrosine]] as [[Precursor (chemistry)|precursors]]. Apart from colchicine and colchicoside, it contains several other alkaloids including gloriosine, [[chelidonic acid]], and [[salicylic acid]].{{cite web |url=http://www.inchem.org/documents/pims/plant/pim245.htm |title=''Gloriosa superba'' |publisher= [[International Programme on Chemical Safety]] |first1=R. |last1=Fernando |first2=D. |last2=Widyaratna |year=1989 }} The young leaves and seeds contain a higher concentration of colchicine, with the seeds containing a colchicine content that is two to five times higher than in the tuber. [[β-Sitosterol]], a [[fatty acid]], and [[glucoside]]s are found in the flowers. Due to the presence of colchicine, most parts of the plant are [[toxic]], especially the seeds and the tubers. The plant parts or derived compounds are [[poisonous]] and ingestion can be fatal to humans, [[fish]], [[cattle]], and other domesticated animals.{{cite web |url=http://www.aspca.org/Pet-care/poison-control/Plants/gloriosa_lily.aspx |title=Gloriosa Lily |publisher=[[American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals]] |access-date=1 June 2026 }} Poisonings also occur as the tubers are mistaken for [[sweet potato]] or [[Yam (vegetable)|yam]] and consumed.{{cite journal |last1=Gooneratne |first1=B. W. M. |title=Massive generalized alopecia after poisoning by ''Gloriosa superba'' |journal=British Medical Journal |date=1966 |volume=1966 |issue=5494 |pages=1023–1024 |doi=10.1136/bmj.1.5494.1023 |pmid=5909848 |pmc=1844473}} About {{cvt|60|mg}} of colchicine is considered lethal to humans, while deaths have occured at lower does, and people have survived after ingesting doses of up to {{cvt|350|mg}}. Research has indicated that the [[median lethal dose]] was 5 mg per kg in rats. Colchicine is absorbed in the [[gastrointestinal tract]]. It affects the [[cell membrane]] and disrupts [[cell division]]. The symptoms of poisoning can show up two to six hours after ingestion. Symptoms include [[nausea]], [[vomiting]], burning in the throat, abdominal pain, [[convulsion]]s, and [[diarrhea]]. It leads to drop of [[blood pressure]], difficulty in breathing, and loss of consciousness, which may progress to [[haematuria]], [[oliguria]], [[leucocytosis]], [[leucopenia]], [[thrombocytopenia]], and [[haemorrhage]]. [[Polyneuropathy]] and muscle weakness occur later, followed by death by respiratory distress or cardiovascular failure in a few days if left untreated. It is also known to cause late [[alopecia]].{{cite journal |last1=Gooneratne |first1=B. W. M. |title=Massive generalized alopecia after poisoning by ''Gloriosa superba'' |journal=British Medical Journal |date=1966 |volume=1966 |issue=5494 |pages=1023–1024 |doi=10.1136/bmj.1.5494.1023 |pmid=5909848 |pmc=1844473}} There is no known [[antidote]] to Gloriosa poisoning. While it is toxic to humans and most animals, the poison had shown no effect on some [[mammals]] such as [[African porcupine]] and certain species of [[Mole (animal)|mole]]s. ==Uses== [[File:Gloriosa superba-1-Anna park-yercaud-salem-India.JPG|thumb|The [[tuber]]s are used extensively in [[traditional medicine]]]] It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] for its varied colored flowers. As it contains colchicine, it is widely used in [[pharmaceuticals]].{{cite journal |last1=Ade |first1=Ravindra |last2=Rai |first2=Mahendra K. |title=Review: Current advances in ''Gloriosa superba'' L. |journal=Biodiversitas |date=2009 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=210–214 |doi=10.13057/biodiv/d100409 |doi-access=free |url=http://biodiversitas.mipa.uns.ac.id/D/D1004/D100409.pdf }} Colchicine is used in the treatment of [[gout]], and other [[inflammatory disorders]]. Colchicine has also used in experimental research to slow [[cell division]], finding application in [[oncology]]. The plant derivatives are used in [[arrow poison]] in Africa, and [[snake]] repellent in India. The plant is extensively used in traditional medicine such as [[ayurveda]]. It has been used to as a [[laxative]], and to treat [[ulcers]], [[arthritis]], [[haemorrhoid]]s, [[cholera]], [[infertility]], [[intestinal worms]], [[colic]], renal ailments, [[snake bite]], [[typhus]], [[leprosy]], and other dermatological conditions. In Africa, the parts of the plant are used to treat various ailments. The leaves are used for treating [[asthma]] in Democractic Republic of Congo, and [[rheumatism]] in Burundi. The extract from the leaves are used to treat [[cough]], and pain in Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso, and as a [[disinfectant]] and anti-[[malaria]] drug in Tanzania. The tuber extract is used as a sleep inducer in Sudan, and to treat abdominal disorders in Kenya and Congo. It is also ued to treat ear ache in Tanzania and tooth ache in Zimbabwe. Apart from traditional uses, the plant and its derivatives has been used to commit [[murder]], [[suicide]], to induce [[abortion]]s and to poison animals such as [[dog]]s. == Culture and symbolism == [[File:Gloriosa superba Indonesia Stamp 1966.jpg|thumb|upright=0.5|''Gloriosa superba'' on an Indonesian stamp (1966)]] ''Gloriosa superba'' is the [[National symbols of Zimbabwe|national flower]] of Zimbabwe.{{cite web |last=Mpofu |first=Thulani |url=https://www.thenationalnews.com/world/africa/zimbabwe-s-national-flower-faces-extinction-1.497350/ |title=Zimbabwe's national flower faces extinction |work=[[The National (Abu Dhabi)|The National]] |date=26 February 2010 |access-date=1 June 2026 }} In 1947, [[Elizabeth II]] received a diamond [[brooch]] in the shape of the flower for her twenty-first birthday while traveling to [[Rhodesia]].{{cite web |url=http://www.royalcollection.org.uk/microsites/queenandcommonwealth/MicroObject.asp?row=92&themeid=944&item=92 |title=Flame Lily Brooch, 1947 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927145533/http://www.royalcollection.org.uk/microsites/queenandcommonwealth/MicroObject.asp?row=92&themeid=944&item=92 |archive-date=27 September 2013 |work=[[The Royal Collection Trust]] }} The flower is known by various names in [[Tamil language|Tamil]] including Chenkaanthal and [[Karthigai]] Poo (flower blooming in the [[Tamil calendar]] month of Karthigai) in [[Tamil language|Tamil]].{{cite web|url=https://forests.tn.gov.in/pages/view/state_symbols|title=State symbols|work=[[Tamil Nadu Forest Department]], [[Government of Tamil Nadu]]|access-date=1 August 2026}}{{cite news |title=Karthigaipoo declared as National flower of Eelam Tamils |url=https://tamilnet.com/art.html?catid=79&artid=11322 |work=Tamil Net |date=14 April 2004 |access-date=1 June 2026}} It is the [[List of Tamil Nadu state symbols|state flower]] of the Indian state of [[Tamil Nadu]].{{cite web|url=https://knowindia.gov.in/national-identity-elements/states-ut-symbol-s-z.php|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170908003348/http://knowindia.gov.in/national-identity-elements/states-ut-symbol-s-z.php|url-status=dead|archive-date=8 September 2017|title=States and Union Territories symbols|work=[[Government of India]]|access-date=18 April 2020}} As per the [[Government of Tamil Nadu]], it was designated so because of its association with Tamil culture and its medicinal usage. The flower was designated as the national flower of the ''de facto'' state of [[Tamil Eelam]] by the [[Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam]] in 2003, as it contained the colours of the Tamil Eelam flag and because it bloomed during November, coinciding with [[Maaveerar Naal]]. ==Notes== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Gloriosa superba}} * {{AfricanPlants|Gloriosa superba}} * [http://flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Glory%20Lily.html ''Gloriosa superba''] at Flowers of India {{Rhodesian topics}} {{Tamil Nadu}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q2175092}} [[Category:Colchicaceae]] [[Category:Flora of Africa]] [[Category:Flora of China]] [[Category:Flora of tropical Asia]] [[Category:Medicinal plants]] [[Category:Garden plants]] [[Category:National symbols of Rhodesia]] [[Category:National symbols of Zimbabwe]] [[Category:Plants described in 1753]] [[Category:Botanical taxa named by Carl Linnaeus]]
